paper_title: DeOverlay: A Benchmark and Source-Anchored Flow for Video Overlay Removal

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video overlay removal aims to recover scenes obscured by subtitles, titles, and logos while preserving surrounding content. Existing methods use temporal propagation or source-conditioned generation, but can leave residual overlays and distort scene structure when useful source information is obscured. We propose DeOverlay, a source-anchored flow model that reconstructs the clean video from the source latent with fixed source guidance. Specifically, we train a shared velocity network along paired source-to-clean paths using region-weighted flow matching, enabling successive cor- rections from intermediate states. To select local source cues, we develop visibility-normalized temporal aggregation that excludes masked positions and averages the remaining observations. Global source context and edit-region embeddings complement these cues through additive condi- tioning, retaining a single video-token sequence. To evaluate scene recovery across diverse overlay conditions, we introduce DVTE-Bench, comprising 1,631 paired videos across eight text-overlay categories, with OCR-screened clean targets, frame-aligned pixel masks, and a common evaluation protocol. Experiments on the complete release show that DeOverlay outperforms four baselines on all five reconstruction and perceptual metrics, reducing Mask LPIPS and Mask VFID by 58.3% and 70.3%, respectively, relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. Additional qualitative examples demonstrate the removal of graphic logos and stickers. We will make the complete benchmark, evaluation code, and test outputs availabl. Project page:https://yahooo-m.github.io/DVTE-Bench/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Video overlay removal aims to recover scene content obscured by subtitles, titles, watermarks, and logos while leaving the surrounding video unchanged. Although neighboring frames may reveal some occluded content, persistent coverage leaves other regions unobserved throughout the clip. Effective removal therefore requires both exploiting available observations and inferring missing content, while maintaining temporal coherence and preserving the scene structure already present in the input. Propagation-based inpainting transfers image content and features across frames, but relies on learned priors when covered regions lack direct observations [19]. Generative methods infer covered content through subtitle-specific reconstruction [5] or noise-initialized editing, in which source information enters through 1 Figure 1 Starting state and source conditioning. Channeland sequence-conditioned editors start from noise, whereas ours starts from zs and receives fixed source features at each update. On shared patch grid, the three designs use , 2N , and video tokens per call, with auxiliary tokens and codecs omitted from the diagram. channel concatenation [20] or sequence concatenation [8] while the editable state begins from noise. Our paired comparisons show residual lettering and boundary distortions in some evaluated outputs (Figure 4). We propose DeOverlay, which starts reconstruction from the source latent and keeps the original source available to each update. shared velocity network learns source-to-clean corrections from paired latent paths under region-weighted flow objective, then applies successive corrections at inference as the state and time evolve under fixed weights and source guidance. Visibility-normalized temporal aggregation averages unmasked source features across nearby frames, while global source summary supplies scene context and an edit-region embedding marks the covered region. By adding these terms to the editing tokens at every update, we keep the source available without second video-token sequence. Where no frame reveals the covered content, the video prior infers it. Evaluating overlay removal requires checking whether the recovered content agrees with the underlying scene. Existing studies assess subtitle erasure [5] or visible watermark removal [1] in separate task-specific settings. To support common regional evaluation across overlay conditions, we introduce DVTE-Bench, the Diverse Video Text Erasure Benchmark, with 1,631 paired videos covering eight text-overlay categories that vary in layout, persistence, and appearance. OCR-screened clean targets and aligned pixel masks provide the references for this evaluation. Experiments on the complete release show improvements over four baselines on all five reconstruction and perceptual metrics, while component and step-count studies examine the contribution of source guidance and repeated updates. Our contributions are summarized as: We introduce DVTE-Bench, paired benchmark covering eight text-overlay types with clean targets, aligned pixel masks, and common evaluation of regional reconstruction, perceptual quality, and temporal behavior. We propose DeOverlay, which learns source-to-clean flow with fixed local and global guidance. Source initialization retains observed structure, while visibility-normalized aggregation selects local cues for reconstructing covered regions. We evaluate DeOverlay on all 1,631 released clips and obtain the best results among five methods on all five reconstruction and perceptual metrics. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Video inpainting and overlay removal. ProPainter combines image and feature propagation with mask-guided sparse attention [19]. For subtitle removal, CLEAR learns subtitle representations followed by generative reconstruction and supports mask-free inference [5], while DECO combines frame-wise priors with temporal modeling for visible watermark removal [1]. Our method learns source-to-clean corrections with persistent source guidance. Source-conditioned restoration. SEDiT concatenates fixed source-reference tokens with noise-initialized tokens for one-step subtitle erasure [8]. For space-time super-resolution, DiffST combines input-derived initialization, motion-based frame aggregation, and video-prompt guidance [2]. We adapt its local/global decomposition through visibility-normalized aggregation at fixed coordinates and pooled latent summary, which guide source-initialized state through successive updates. Flow-based editing. Flow matching and rectified flow learn vector fields along prescribed paths [12, 13]. In restoration, IR-Flow learns degraded-to-clean image transport [4], while PCFlow compares observationinitialized unconditional flow with noise-initialized conditional flow [9]. For editing, FlowEdit performs inversion-free flow editing [10], and RFDM predicts residuals relative to preceding outputs for causal video editing [16]. Our paired video flow combines source initialization, fixed source guidance, and regional weighting within pretrained video transformer [14, 15]. Evaluation resources. CLEAR evaluates 400-clip subtitle benchmark [5], while SEDiT introduces VSRBench-400 with clean videos and subtitle masks [8]. In the watermark setting, DECO evaluates stationary and moving watermarks synthesized on YouTube-VOS and DAVIS [1].

sections.title: 3 DVTE-Bench: Diverse Video Text Erasure
sections.content: We construct DVTE-Bench to evaluate overlay removal and scene reconstruction by pairing each overlaid video with clean target and frame-aligned masks. These pairs support common evaluation across overlay layouts, temporal behaviors, and appearances. Table 1 contrasts DVTE-Bench with existing subtitle benchmarks in paired supervision, overlay diversity, and evaluation coverage.

sections.title:
3.1 Challenge Design
The benchmark contains eight overlay types organized around three aspects of reconstruction (Table 7). Spatial
layout determines which scene regions must be recovered, including vertical text, non-bottom placement, and
multiple simultaneous regions. Temporal behavior affects whether nearby frames expose the covered content,
as illustrated by moving text and persistent watermarks. Appearance and coverage vary through standard
subtitles and artistic titles with display typography, outlines, or glow, while speech-aligned captions add
audio-derived content and timing. Because these factors interact within each category, category comparisons
measure coverage across conditions rather than isolated effects.
sections.content: 3 Figure 2 DVTE-Bench construction. Text plans and type-controlled rendering produce aligned source videos, clean targets, and overlay masks. Target-frame OCR screening rejects 569 of 2,200 candidates and retains 1,631 clips. The eight thumbnails show distinct released clips, while the lower-right source, target, and mask form one aligned example.

sections.title: 3.2 Paired Data and Target Quality
sections.content: The release contains 1,631 clips, 136,090 frames, and 91.1 minutes of video, with 1,085 portrait and 546 landscape clips. As outlined in Figure 2, scene-aware text plans or speech transcripts supply overlay content for type-controlled rendering. This rendering retains the original video as the reconstruction target and produces aligned overlay masks, including masks that follow moving text. Language metadata has 11 labels, dominated by Chinese, English, Korean, and Japanese, with the released distributions shown in Figure 6. Because text in reference can be mistaken for an unerased overlay, we screen every target frame with OCR and reject candidates with confirmed text, removing 569 of 2,200 candidates and retaining 1,631 (74.1%). Preservation of natural scene text requires separate evaluation setting.

sections.title: 3.3 Regional Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: All five methods are evaluated on the same 1,631 released clips, with scoring based on pixel-accurate GT masks from the released NPZ archives independently of the bounding-box masks supplied to mask-conditioned models. Mask PSNR measures pixel fidelity, and Mask SSIM [17] averages the SSIM map over GT mask pixels. Mask LPIPS [18], DISTS [3], and VFID measure perceptual agreement with clean targets. For these perceptual metrics, exterior prediction pixels are replaced by the target, and shared crop covers the union of mask locations over time to focus evaluation on the overlay region. Frame measurements are averaged within videos and then equally across videos, whereas VFID is global distance between video-feature distributions. Infinite-PSNR videos are omitted from the finite PSNR mean and counted as N. Temporal evaluation reports mask-restricted TWE for predictions and clean targets, their aggregate gap, and auxiliary TC and flow statistics using the released Farneback protocol. These diagnostics complement targetreferenced fidelity because temporally smooth outputs can still reconstruct the wrong content. Appendix describes the regional computations and aggregation. 4 Figure 3 DeOverlay overview. (a) Shared-weight Euler updates start from the source latent, with the upper bypass carrying the current state and the lower loop updating state and time with fixed source cues. (b) Visibility-aware source aggregation (VSA), global source conditioning (GSC), and mask embeddings form the source condition. (c) Source cues are added to the current state tokens before joint videotext processing. Tensor grids and intermediate states are schematic, whereas RGB frames are matched source/output pairs.

sections.title: 4 DeOverlay: Source-Anchored Flow
sections.content: Given an overlaid video, removal instruction, and an edit mask, we encode the source as the initial editing state and use shared velocity network to predict corrections with fixed local and global source guidance. video decoder then maps the updated latent to the reconstructed video (Figure 3).

sections.title: 5.2 Reconstruction across Diverse Overlays
sections.content: On all 1,631 released videos, DeOverlay achieves the best results on all five reconstruction and perceptual metrics  (Table 2)  . Compared with MiniMax-Remover, the strongest baseline on these metrics, it improves Mask PSNR from 26.17 to 30.80 dB and SSIM from 0.8044 to 0.8822, while reducing LPIPS, DISTS, and VFID by 58.3%, 40.8%, and 70.3%, respectively. These improvements support more faithful covered-region reconstruction. Coverage across overlay conditions. DeOverlay achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and DISTS across all eight overlay types (Appendix D). Artistic titles produce its lowest PSNR/SSIM (26.24 dB/0.8409), whereas vertical text produces its highest LPIPS/DISTS (0.0975/0.1015). The most difficult category therefore depends on whether pixel accuracy or perceptual similarity is measured. Temporal behavior. Table 2(b) reports the released temporal diagnostics alongside reconstruction fidelity, with DeOverlay obtaining TWE Pred of 9.3110 and TC of 4.2498, compared with ProPainters 8.1428 and 4.0349. All methods use the same mask-restricted computation and clean-target reference of 9.3228. Under this computation, ProPainter and MiniMax-Remover score below the reference despite weaker reconstruction, illustrating why the diagnostic is interpreted together with clean-target fidelity. Appendix specifies the temporal computations. 7 Figure 4 Paired benchmark comparisons. Five frame-40 examples with shared yellow crop boxes compare four baselines, DeOverlay, and clean targets, with inference settings and expanded seven-category comparisons in Appendix E. Figure 5 Removal across overlay appearances. Twelve matched source/output crops cover subtitles, titles, watermarks, sticker, and television logo, with full frames and crop boxes in Appendix E. DeOverlay has an aggregate TWE Gap of 0.0118, versus 0.6133 for MiniMax-Remover and 1.1801 for ProPainter, where the gap compares dataset-level means under the aggregation rule in Appendix I. The five target-referenced metrics in Table 2(a) therefore provide the primary reconstruction comparison, while Flow Mean, Flow Var, and TC retain their released labels and scales as supplementary descriptions of the evaluated outputs. Qualitative reconstruction. Across the five paired examples with clean targets in Figure 4, residual text, blurred structures, and altered colors distinguish the outputs, while DeOverlay more closely preserves the target appearance. In the artistic-title example, the restored car and road remain aligned with the clean target. The multiple-region and non-bottom-text examples also make color shifts and damaged background boundaries visible around the building and clouds, complementing the aggregate scores by showing which structures are recovered within the covered regions. Figure 5 adds twelve application examples spanning subtitle languages and density, title layouts, watermarks, sticker, and television logo. sections.title: 5.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Ablations use 200 randomly sampled DVTE-Bench videos, whereas Table 2 uses all 1,631 videos. Component variants use = 4, with direct-residual reference at = 1, and the step sweep holds the checkpoint fixed. We measure ablation SSIM with MaskCrop SSIM. Effect of source representation and guidance. Replacing source initialization and additive guidance with noise initialization and concatenated source tokens decreases Mask PSNR by 2.861 dB  (Table 3)  . Because the starting state and conditioning change together, this comparison evaluates their combined design. Within the source-initialized model, keeping only the mask embedding reduces PSNR by 0.231 dB, while removing VSA or GSC reduces it by 0.091 or 0.171 dB. These changes show that both local observations and global context contribute to the measured reconstruction quality. Replacing visibility-normalized aggregation with an ordinary temporal mean reduces PSNR by 0.101 dB and raises MAE to 4.360, supporting the use of visibility selection in local aggregation. Increasing from two to four steps within the same checkpoint improves Mask PSNR Effect of flow step count. from 32.410 to 32.461 dB, lowers MAE from 4.330 to 4.299, and improves Crop SSIM and TWE gap  (Table 4)  . Eight steps add only 0.007 dB over four at 1.50 latency, favoring four steps for these component studies. Training formulation and repeated updates. Four-step flow exceeds the separately trained direct-residual reference by 1.161 dB in Mask PSNR, with lower MAE and higher Crop SSIM  (Table 3)  . Each flow update recomputes the velocity from the current state and time with fixed source cues, allowing different inference budgets without retraining.

sections.title: 6 Limitations
sections.content: DVTE-Bench focuses on synthetic text overlays, leaving graphic logos, stickers, and preservation of natural scene text for broader paired evaluation. When neighboring frames provide no visible evidence for fully covered background, reconstruction depends on the video prior. The application examples also include residual graphics and local texture artifacts (Appendix E).

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced DVTE-Bench and DeOverlay for reconstructing scenes beneath video text overlays, with DVTE-Bench unifying eight overlay categories in 1,631 paired videos. Clean targets, aligned pixel masks, and common evaluation protocol support comparisons across overlay layouts, temporal behavior, and appearance. DeOverlay combines source initialization with visibility-normalized local aggregation and global source guidance, keeping the source available through additive conditioning throughout shared-weight flow updates using one video-token sequence. It outperforms four baselines on all five reconstruction and perceptual metrics, and on the 200-video subset, four-step flow exceeds the separately trained direct-residual reference by 1.161 dB in Mask PSNR. Component ablations support both guidance branches, while category-level evaluation separates the challenges of pixel reconstruction and perceptual quality, with artistic titles and vertical text stressing different metrics. Together, the benchmark and method enable joint study of scene recovery and inference cost.

sections.content: The component and step-count ablations use 200 randomly sampled videos from DVTE-Bench, while the main comparison in Table 2 evaluates all 1,631 released videos. F.1 Training Formulation and Initialization Under the same experimental environment, we independently train one-step direct-residual baseline to predict the source-to-target residual. The Gaussian-start model in Table 3 is trained for noise-initialized, two-video-stream input, so its 2.861 dB gap to the source-initialized model reflects both the starting state and the way source evidence enters the network. sections.title: I Temporal Diagnostic Computation
sections.content: Table 2(b) reports the releases temporal measurements on all 1,631 videos, with the TWE label following the forward-flow remap convention specified in the release metadata. Using forward displacement ut1t, the referenced computation samples the previous frame as t1(x) = It1(x + ut1t(x)) (16) and averages its absolute RGB difference from It(x) on the scoring region. This forward-displacement sampling diagnostic differs from backward warping of the previous frame into the current frame, which samples with utt1. The table retains the released diagnostic names and numerical scales, including the reported labels for TC, Flow Mean, and Flow Var. The aggregate gap applies the absolute value after video-level averaging, TWEpred TWEGT, with cleantarget reference 9.3228, so opposite signed deviations can cancel. Table 2 also reports the target-referenced reconstruction comparison.
